nodes.label: W. E. B. Du Bois
nodes.description: Historian and social investigator whose selected works move between documentary history, an urban survey and the form of the essay. The 1896 slave-trade monograph begins from laws and official records while acknowledging weak economic evidence. The Souls of Black Folk (1903) articulates double consciousness. Chad Williams reads Black Reconstruction (1935) as a history of Black political agency and defeated multiracial democracy; Elijah Anderson rereads the Philadelphia survey as an account of racial exclusion. Hartman’s later criticism of the survey’s class and gender judgments is recorded as a distinct disagreement.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Suppression of the African Slave-Trade (1896); The Philadelphia Negro (1899; Isabel Eaton’s domestic-service investigation separately credited); The Souls of Black Folk (1903); Black Reconstruction (1935). Readers: Chad Williams (online 2022, print 2023), Elijah Anderson (2023), Saidiya Hartman (2020).

nodes.scope_note: Read in part: the 1896 preface and chapter I opening, and the 1903 Forethought and chapter I, in public-domain transcriptions. The 1899 and 1935 books are known here through the named readings by Anderson and Williams. Their conclusions are attributed to them. Hartman’s criticism comes from her 2020 interview, not a newly read passage of Wayward Lives. Period racial/evolutionary vocabulary is historical evidence, not endorsed terminology. Later activism and writings are not comprehensively surveyed. Existing edge_241 retains its Du Bois/Gilroy diaspora-resource claim; no duplicate personal Atlantic arrow is added.

nodes.label: Carter G. Woodson
nodes.description: Historian and educator whose research programme joined scholarly publication to community historical education. His education study recovered efforts before emancipation; the 1918 migration synthesis placed wartime departures in a longer history of seeking refuge. The Mis-Education of the Negro (1933) criticized schooling that produced dependence while excluding Black history. The Journal of Negro History and Negro History Week gave this project different scholarly and public forms. Pyne’s institutional retrospective also records disagreement over foundation funding and independence; neither celebration nor the title “father of Black history” establishes sole authorship of the field.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Education of the Negro Prior to 1861 (1915; 1919 preface consulted); Journal of Negro History (1916); A Century of Negro Migration (1918); Associated Publishers (1921); Negro History Week (1926); The Mis-Education of the Negro (1933).

nodes.scope_note: Own words read: the 1919 education preface/opening, the 1918 migration preface/opening and the 1933 preface/chapter I in transcriptions. Original/edition dates remain distinct. Pyne’s Library of Congress essay and the NPS supply mediated institutional history, community support and public statements. Pyne contrasts Woodson’s account of obstructive fundraising with Meier/Rudwick’s and Winston’s readings; those underlying studies were not independently read here. Most book chapters and the complete journal remain unread. Public-history placement describes a specific educational practice, not later professional membership.

nodes.label: Darlene Clark Hine
nodes.description: Historian of Black women, work and professional institutions. In her 1989 essay Hine argued that migration and institutional histories require attention to sexual violence and a protective culture of dissemblance, while acknowledging limits in this explanation. Celia J. Wintz reads Black Women in White (1989) as a revisionist nursing history centered on racial and gender barriers. Hine’s 2003 opening meta-argument places parallel Black professional organizations within the conditions of resistance to white supremacy. These are distinct historical explanations, rather than an assertion that all Black women shared one experience or method.

Reader: Celia J. Wintz (1991).

nodes.label: Saidiya Hartman
nodes.description: Scholar of African American literature and cultural history who makes slavery’s afterlives and the conditions of historical narration central problems. Her 2008 essay joins critical fabulation to restraint and the acknowledgment of unrecoverable lives. In her own account of Wayward Lives, ordinary young Black women are social thinkers and experimenters, rather than pathological cases in state records. Respect and criticism coexist in her reading of Du Bois: she values his intellectual achievement while questioning the Philadelphia survey’s class and gender judgments.

nodes.label: Marisa J. Fuentes
nodes.description: Historian of slavery, gender and the Caribbean whose work asks what archival violence permits historians to know. Her 2010 abstract challenges triumphalist accounts of Rachael Pringle Polgreen by examining power over other women. The read excerpt from Dispossessed Lives (2016) explains the limits of recovering enslaved women’s perspectives and the need to change the archival gaze. With Deborah Gray White, Fuentes coedited the collective Scarlet and Black project at Rutgers. Her 2017 AAIHS essay connects this methodological problem with contemporary studies of slavery and capitalism and explicitly acknowledges Hartman’s essay as inspiration for a jointly edited project.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Power and Historical Figuring” (2010); Dispossessed Lives (2016); with Deborah Gray White, editor, Scarlet and Black, Volume 1 (2016); with Brian Connolly, editor, the History of the Present slavery/archive issue (2016); “A Violent and Violating Archive” (2017).

edges.relationship: Black Reconstruction (1935) reinterprets emancipation and Reconstruction through Black agency and an interrupted experiment in multiracial democracy, as Chad Williams reads it (2022).
edges.evidence_note: Williams’s introduction, read, supplies this characterization; the full 1935 book is not newly read. The existing field roster is retained, and this contribution does not claim sole founding of Black historical scholarship.

edges.relationship: The Philadelphia Negro (1899) examines a specific Black urban community; Elijah Anderson’s 2023 introduction emphasizes employment discrimination and the limits of expecting reform from informed employers.
edges.evidence_note: A named reader’s interpretation of the 1899 Philadelphia survey. This is a contribution through one study, not a claim that Du Bois founded all urban history. Isabel Eaton’s domestic-service study is separately credited; it is not treated as Du Bois’s sole-authored research.

edges.relationship: Independent historical research and publishing: antebellum education (1915), the Journal of Negro History (1916), migration history (1918), and a critique of educational dependence (1933).
edges.evidence_note: The 1919 education preface, 1918 migration preface/opening, and 1933 preface/chapter I were read. Pyne and the NPS supply institutional dates. Earlier Black historical organizations and community support preclude a sole-founder claim.

edges.relationship: Negro History Week (1926) combines public historical education with the research and publishing programme supported by Black communities.
edges.evidence_note: Pyne’s LOC essay describes the programme and community financing; the NPS reproduces Woodson’s public-education statement. This is a documented commemorative/educational practice predating the later professional label public history, not self-identification with that profession or sole invention of commemoration.

edges.relationship: The culture of dissemblance: sexual violence, privacy and Black women’s migration require analytical explanation beyond the recovery of prominent lives (1989).
edges.evidence_note: Own essay, pp.912–916 and 919–920 read. Hine treats sexual/personal motives as additions to economic explanations and acknowledges that dissemblance can be mistaken for control over hostile representations. Her historical generalizations are not universal findings for all Black women.

edges.relationship: Black Women in White (1989) studies Black nurses’ struggles against racial and gender exclusion; Hine’s later argument makes parallel professional organizations important to resistance (2003).
edges.evidence_note: The nursing-book interpretation is attributed to Celia J. Wintz’s read repository abstract; the book is not newly read. Hine’s 2003 published opening extract, rather than the whole address, supplies the parallel-institutions argument. A scoped contribution to nursing/professional history, not founding medical history.

edges.relationship: Critical fabulation confronts the violence of slavery’s archive while requiring narrative restraint and acknowledging the failure to recover the dead (2008).
edges.evidence_note: Hartman’s pp.9 and 11–14, read. She distinguishes speculation from verified recovery and refuses closure; no claim that invention supplies lost testimony is accepted. This personal methodological contribution is different from the existing aggregate archive-to-Atlantic and archive-to-Black-history arrows.

edges.relationship: Wayward Lives (2019) places ordinary young Black women’s experiments in living at the center of historical explanation, while refusing to reproduce state case files’ pathologizing judgments.
edges.evidence_note: The book’s method is read through Hartman’s 2020 first-person interviews and the 2019 institutional account, not a new whole-book reading. This contribution concerns women’s history and its subjects; the generic archive/Atlantic relationships are retained separately.

edges.relationship: Hartman admires Du Bois’s intellectual achievement but criticizes the Philadelphia survey’s elite and Victorian judgments about Black intimate life (2020 interview).
edges.evidence_note: Explicit first-person answer to Yannise Jean about Du Bois, read. The criticism is dated to the 2020 interview and limited to these class/gender judgments, rather than a wholesale rejection of Du Bois or a passage independently checked in the 2019 book.

edges.relationship: Dispossessed Lives (2016) studies the production of archival silence and changes the narrative gaze toward enslaved women, while refusing a claim of complete recovery.
edges.evidence_note: The publisher-authorized book excerpt and interview, read, support the method; the 2010 abstract supplies an earlier distinct challenge to triumphalist representations of Polgreen. The whole book remains unread; unnamed objections are Fuentes’s report, not independently read replies.

edges.relationship: With Deborah Gray White and a collective of researchers, Scarlet and Black (2016) brings Rutgers’s involvement in slavery and dispossession into the university’s public history.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description and contents, read, establish a jointly edited committee publication with separately named chapter authors. White wrote its introduction; Fuentes is neither sole author nor sole discoverer. Contribution is scoped to this collaborative publication and stated public purpose, not a general claim to founding public history.

edges.relationship: Hartman’s “Venus in Two Acts” is explicitly named as inspiration for Connolly and Fuentes’s 2016 slavery/archive special issue, as Fuentes reports in 2017.
edges.evidence_note: Fuentes’s AAIHS essay explicitly identifies Hartman’s essay as inspiration. Fuentes’s author bibliography establishes Connolly’s coeditorship and 2016; USF corroborates their joint introduction in Fall 2016. Influence is limited to that collaborative project, not Hartman as sole source of Fuentes’s work or agreement on every method. The full issue remains unread.

rationale: Each promoted person retains an existing identity and receives at least two evidence-scoped relationships and three dated contribution events.
